title: Replicating Compute-Disclosure Tracking on Open Model Releases to Test Reporting Consistency

# Replicating Compute-Disclosure Tracking on Open Model Releases to Test Reporting Consistency

**Problem:** Compute governance relies on knowing training-compute figures, and Epoch AI tracks these for frontier models. But for the rapidly-growing set of open-weight releases, training-compute and dataset-size disclosures are inconsistent or absent, undermining any compute-threshold-based regulation (e.g., EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOP threshold) applied to the open ecosystem.

**Direction:** Replicate Epoch-style compute estimation/disclosure tracking, with the twist of focusing on a cohort of recent open-weight releases. For each, record whether training compute is disclosed, estimate it from public params/tokens/hardware when undisclosed, and quantify how many would or wouldn't cross regulatory thresholds and how uncertain those estimates are.

**Why it matters:** Compute-threshold governance is only as good as the disclosures behind it; mapping the open-ecosystem disclosure gap directly informs whether thresholds are enforceable. Pure public-data analysis with simple FLOP estimation, no compute needed.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Epoch AI compute tracking data and EU AI Act compute-threshold (10^25 FLOP) provisions. Twist = applying compute-disclosure tracking to the open-model cohort and quantifying estimation uncertainty.

title: Replicating Model-Spec Honesty/Sycophancy Probes on Open Models With a User-Authority Twist

# Replicating Model-Spec Honesty/Sycophancy Probes on Open Models With a User-Authority Twist

**Problem:** Model specs encode honesty and instruction-hierarchy norms, and spec evals test whether models obey developer over user when they conflict. A governance-relevant failure is sycophancy: models abandoning correct factual stances when a user asserts authority or disagrees. How open models handle the spec's honesty-vs-deference tension is under-measured.

**Direction:** Replicate the spec's honesty/instruction-hierarchy probes on open models, with the twist of systematically varying asserted user authority and disagreement pressure across a fixed factual battery. Measure how often each model abandons a correct answer under pressure (sycophancy rate) versus holding the spec-compliant honest line.

**Why it matters:** Honesty under social pressure is a fuzzy-reward safety property hard to evaluate and easy for labs to under-prioritize; it bears on whether spec-based norms are robust governance instruments. Open spec, open models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in OpenAI Model Spec / model_spec_evals (instruction hierarchy, honesty) and SpecEval (arXiv 2509.02464). Twist = systematic user-authority/disagreement pressure to measure sycophancy against spec.

title: If-Then Commitment Specificity Scorer for Frontier Safety Policies

# If-Then Commitment Specificity Scorer for Frontier Safety Policies

**Problem:** Frontier safety frameworks rely on 'if-then commitments' that trigger mitigations when capability thresholds are crossed, but many are written so vaguely that it is unclear what measurable trigger would fire them. There is no public tool that measures how operationally specific each commitment is.

**Direction:** Build a rubric-driven scorer (e.g. 0=aspirational, 1=qualitative trigger, 2=named eval, 3=quantitative threshold + named eval + bound response) and apply it to the ~12 published frontier safety policies. Use an LLM as a rubric-anchored extractor to pull every if-then clause, then score each on trigger measurability, response bindingness, and timing. Report a per-lab specificity profile and aggregate gaps.

**Why it matters:** Operationalizing safety objectives into measurable deployment triggers is a named open problem. A reproducible specificity metric gives auditors and AISIs a lightweight way to track whether commitments are getting more concrete over time, and is doable entirely from public documents with no lab access.

**Relevant context:** METR's 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies' (2024-2025 updates) catalogues if-then commitments and CCLs; FAR.AI's Painter talk on challenges creating if-then commitments; 'From Principles to Rules' (arXiv 2407.07300). All policies are public PDFs.
